title: The President Is Acting Like He Works for China
text:
Updated at 6:06 p.m. ET on November 23, 2026 

 Americans learned several things over the past few days. The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence , is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation that makes some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. Another is that China’s Communist regime has gotten its hands on the chips. The markets, as usual, have reconfirmed that they prefer profit to politics: Nvidia’s stock price jumped more than 30 percent on the news of Huang’s return.

 But most important, Americans learned—yet again—that their president does not care about the national security of the United States. In fact, he is so aggressively resistant to any notion of security that his actions have become almost indistinguishable from those of a hostile foreign agent.

 Step back for a moment and consider this sequence of events. The married Nvidia boss was caught in a sexual relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. (She is not related to Jensen, but I will use first names here to avoid confusion). Alice, during this affair, worked for Megaspeed, a company in Singapore. Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips, and then found ways to get them to China, despite U.S. export controls. She also reportedly maintained contacts with the Ministry of State Security, the Chinese intelligence agency, while carrying on with Jensen.

 (Some reports call Alice an “agent” or a “spy,” others refer to her as an “asset.” The distinction makes little practical difference in Jensen’s case. Someone who is employed by an intelligence agency, has professional training, and may be acting under a false identity, is an officer . Agents and assets are people recruited from private life, outside of the organization, who have a cooperative relationship, in varying degrees, with such an agency but aren’t actually employed as spooks. Either way, Jensen was literally in bed with someone who was reportedly in bed with Chinese intelligence.)

 [ Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection ] 

 All of this certainly looks bad. It gets worse. The United States government, including President Trump, was warned by American intelligence that Alice was entangled with Beijing. In fact, Trump was warned twice in seven months, including once during a briefing by Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May as Trump was headed to China for a state visit. This must have been awkward, because shortly afterward, Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One and joined the U.S. delegation for the trip to China.

 Trump ignored these warnings—or more accurately, in classic Trump style, he pretended not to know about these issues. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he said, just before his most recent visit to China. “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

 Clearly not. Nor did these warnings move Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, whose former company, Cantor Fitzgerald, has significant ties to Nvidia , including financing some of the firms that were buying its chips.

 The company is now run by Lutnick’s son.

 Trump’s reaction to all this? When Jensen was discovered and had to leave his company, Trump got right to work trying to put him back in the big chair at Nvidia. “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” Nvidia wasn’t having it : Internal sources at the company made clear to reporters that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated.

 So what changed in a matter of days? Nothing, except that the president apparently brought the American intelligence community into the fray to give Jensen a clean bill of health. At least that’s how it sounds from the Nvidia board’s public statement: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

 The national-security process is slow and deliberative for a reason; people with even modest clearances who have been accused of minor infractions have had to wait months, sometimes even going to court, before being allowed back to work. An executive working with some of America’s most exotic technology commits adultery with a foreign citizen who has ties to a hostile government, and is credibly accused of funneling highly restricted American technology to a hostile intelligence service—and the U.S. security mandarins give the guy a thumbs up after a week ?

 Trump likes Jensen, he likes money, he likes the markets, and he likes Lutnick and his family. So perhaps he told the American spooks to sound the all-clear so that Jensen could get back to work. Trump indicated as much today when he told CNBC that he spoke with Nvidia’s board members. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.”

 In a statement on Truth Social, Trump said: “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” That means exactly nothing. Saying that Todd Blanche does not “possess evidence” is an artful formulation meaning that Blanche does not have a file in front of him from the intelligence community detailing Jensen’s acts, some of which might have been dangerous even if they were not “unlawful.” (As any government employee can tell you, any number of “lawful” activities, including carrying lots of debt or having emotional problems, can sink a clearance and a job.) And because of Trump’s pressure to clear Jensen, it’s unlikely he ever will.

 Not only did Trump celebrate the Nvidia decision, but he noted that the board’s action possibly averted a worse outcome: Jensen Huang working for China. If Jensen was “mad” enough, Trump said during an interview today , he might have accepted an offer to lead a Chinese company, because the Nvidia boss has some of their “blood in him.” In other words, the United States just vouched for a man the president said might have defected to China if he hadn’t been given his job back.

 [ Jonathan Chait: Trump’s backing of Huang is not superintelligent ] 

 To recap: After a top industrialist got caught in an affair with a woman who might have been using the affair to slip American technology to a U.S. enemy, the president declared that his own spies had cleared his pal, waved off the national-security damage, and left everyone, ostensibly, happy. And by “everyone,” I mean Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick, Nvidia stockholders, and Communist China.

 Trump solved this problem in a way that would make a foreign spy or a lobbyist for a foreign government both impressed and envious. Enemy spooks, their agents, and their assets spend their lives trying to do what Trump did in a week. Jensen’s off the hook, and the stock has bounced back. (And the Chinese should give Alice a medal.)

 This whole terrible situation shows in galling detail that Trump just doesn’t think very much about the interests of the United States. (It also suggests that he couldn’t care less about the recent election, in which corruption was a top issue for many voters). He makes no secret of his preference for his own relationships over America’s safety: When asked if Russian President Vladimir Putin was a “friend to America,” Trump shrugged and said, “I can’t speak to America. ”

 That’s because Trump, for all his flag-hugging nonsense, doesn’t think in terms of “America” or “China” or “Russia.” He is a globalist, in the very worst sense of the word: a man who cares nothing for states or peoples or ideologies, because he sees the world as just an interconnected group of companies and banks. Some of those companies are run by his friends, and those are the only peers who matter. Everyone else is just raw material or collateral damage; the masses are just ciphers who either obey him or obey someone else.

 It is perhaps an insult to foreign agents to say that Trump is acting like them. Foreign agents work for countries, and care about them. They do what they do out of patriotism, however misguided they may be about the regimes they might serve. Trump has no such ideals. Trump’s business is Trump’s business, and everything else—including “national interest” and “national security”—are just meaningless phrases used by chumps and saps.

 This article was updated to clarify the words agent , officer , and asset .
